part_title: Clear Prompts, Context and Negative Instructions
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 01–04 individually, including specific prompt text, service examples, diagram stages, exclusions and output samples; narration follows those exact visuals.

scenes.title: Prompt engineering: give the model a clear task
scenes.narration: This slide contrasts a vague prompt with a useful one. On the left, 'Summarize AWS' leaves the model guessing what content, audience and level of detail you want. The example answer is a general description of AWS, not necessarily a summary of your article. Now read the center panel: the improved prompt has four parts. First, its instruction is to summarize key points. Second, it supplies the actual article as context. Third, it specifies a beginner who is new to cloud computing. Fourth, it asks for three to five plain-language bullet points. The sample text below combines all four into a real prompt. Follow the arrow to the right: instead of a broad statement, the result is a structured list of key points from the supplied article. Those bracketed key points are placeholders, not actual article claims. The important technical distinction is in the bottom-left note: a prompt guides inference, the moment a trained model produces an answer; it does not update the model's learned weights. If the audience changes to an experienced architect, we can change the prompt rather than retrain the model. Always inspect the answer for accuracy and whether it follows the requested format.

scenes.title: Build an enhanced prompt
scenes.narration: Here is a practical way to build and test a prompt. Start with the four elements on the left. Task tells the model what work to do. Context provides the source material. Audience identifies who needs the explanation. Output constraints specify structure and style. The center card shows all four in one prompt: 'Using the supplied article,' explain Amazon S3 'to a beginner,' 'in three bullets,' and 'use plain English.' Notice the colored labels connecting each phrase back to its purpose. S3 is Amazon's object-storage service, used to store files and other objects in cloud buckets; the slide is asking for an accessible explanation rather than complex configuration details. The right panel illustrates an answer organized around Purpose, Use case and Limitation. This is a sample structure, not an actual verified S3 explanation. The final step is to review the response: does it correctly explain the service, use exactly three bullets, and avoid confusing beginners? If the result misses the use case, adjust the instruction or add better source context. Prompt engineering is an iterative process of giving clear requirements, testing the response and refining what the model receives.

scenes.title: Negative prompting: specify exclusions
scenes.narration: Negative prompting means specifying what the model should leave out, while still giving it a clear positive task. Look at the first panel's instruction: summarize the provided AWS article for beginners, but omit pricing estimates and promotional claims. In the second panel, the funnel separates relevant material, marked with a green check, from excluded content with a red cross. The third panel shows the intended short, beginner-friendly AI summary. The list on the right makes the boundary concrete. Key concepts, high-level explanations, beginner use cases and considerations are allowed. Speculative prices, sales slogans such as 'industry leading,' and special offers are excluded. This is useful if you are writing neutral study material rather than marketing copy. But read the warning under the title: exclusions are instructions, not a security boundary. A generative model may still ignore them or produce an unsupported claim. Therefore review the result, and use appropriate application validation and safety controls when exclusions are critical. The goal is to reduce irrelevant output, not to pretend that a sentence beginning with 'do not' guarantees compliance.

scenes.title: Negative prompt: a worked AWS summary
scenes.narration: Now we can inspect an actual example from beginning to end. The source-data column lists four AWS services: EC2 for compute, S3 for storage, RDS for managed databases and Lambda for serverless functions. It also mentions introductory learning resources and certifications. The second column defines the task: summarize this text for beginners in two or three sentences, covering the core services and learning benefits. The red exclusions column says to leave out technical configuration, named tutorials, personal stories, unsupported pricing and speculation. Finally, the green response panel illustrates a concise two-sentence answer. It mentions EC2, S3, RDS and Lambda, then explains that beginners can use introductory resources and later consider certifications. Why is that better than blindly copying the source? It retains the important ideas while removing details outside the requested scope. Equally, a negative prompt should not delete vital qualifications merely to make the answer shorter. In this example, verify that all listed services are described correctly and that no invented prices appear. The four panels together demonstrate source material, instructions, exclusions and a reviewed output.
